rationale: The statement is the standard interchange law for a finite double sum, specialised to the library's enumeration-defined sums over arbitrary finite index sets and stated simultaneously for natural- and real-valued summands. That merge and the explicit bridge between the two sum notions make it a semantic-source rather than an exact-source case. The proof's finite-reindexing construction is local.

Finite incidence relations, their row and column fibres, and counting incidences by either family are the standard relation form of double counting. The item packages the data and notation before the subsequent theorem and uses a subset of A times B rather than a matrix or bipartite graph, so it is renotated and reorganised. This definition has no separate proof component.

The equality obtained by counting a finite incidence set by its first- and second-coordinate fibres is the standard double-counting principle. The local statement is cast in the preceding fibre notation and carries both natural and canonically embedded real equalities, so it is a semantic restatement. Its two fibre-partition counts follow the sourced standard argument, adapted to this library's finite-sum API.

The conclusion that one finite fibre is at least the average fibre size is the standard averaging principle. The item expresses it through an incidence relation, the canonical embedding of natural counts into R, and a quotient by |B|, with an explicit nonempty-index hypothesis. The contradiction proof from double counting and finite-sum monotonicity is locally written.

The least natural q with m <= nq is the standard ceiling of m/n for n positive. The item deliberately defines only this natural quotient-ceiling, develops its minimality and bounding consequences in the library's Peano arithmetic, and then records its real quotient inequality; these convention and interface choices go beyond the generic sourced definition. The inline well-ordering verification belongs to the definition, so there is no separate proof component.

The source gives the generalized pigeonhole conclusion that distributing more than ell times n objects among n containers forces more than ell in one container. The item gives the equivalent fibre-counting form and adds the ceiling formulation, including explicit empty-domain and nonempty-codomain boundary readings. The contradiction-by-summing-fibres proof is the standard argument, adapted to local cardinal and ceiling notation.

A finite family of subsets, all subfamily intersections, the union, and the trace of a point are standard data for inclusion-exclusion. This item packages them into a named 'sieve family', explicitly stipulates the empty intersection relative to an ambient set, and records several finiteness and trace conventions. Those packaging choices make it a semantic-source case. It has no separate proof component.

The finite-family alternating intersection formula for a union and its complementary 'none of the events' form are the standard inclusion-exclusion identities with the same hypotheses and direction; only notation and the canonical embedding of counts into R differ cosmetically. The proof is adapted from the standard pointwise-indicator argument, with local finite-sum interchange and empty-index bookkeeping made explicit.

The source states the exact identity sum_{i=0}^ell (-1)^i binom(n,i) = (-1)^ell binom(n-1,ell) for n at least 1 and ell below n. Relabelling n as t and ell as m-1 gives precisely the item's statement, including its range. The induction from Pascal's rule is a standard sourced proof pattern, expanded into the library's zero-based finite-sum conventions.

Both sources state the alternating Bonferroni truncations with odd truncations above the union size and even truncations below it, together with exactness when all available levels are included. This is exactly the three-clause theorem after translating notation. The proof follows the standard pointwise binomial-prefix argument and is adapted to the page's sieve and finite-sum interfaces.

The source gives the standard inclusion-exclusion formula for the number of surjections, sum_j (-1)^j binom(k,j)(k-j)^n. The item states it for all natural n and k, embeds the count in R, and spells out all three zero-parameter cases under the convention 0^0=1; those boundary and typing additions make the match semantic rather than exact. Its proof is the standard missing-value sieve argument adapted to the local function-set and finite-sum notation.

The derangement number is standardly the number of permutations of n objects with no fixed point, exactly the set-cardinality definition used here. The initial values are direct readings of that definition and do not alter it. This is a definition with no separate proof component.

The source gives D_n = n! sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k/k!, equivalently sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k binom(n,k)(n-k)!, with the same natural range and the empty-permutation value. That is the item's statement after its zero-based indexing and canonical embedding. The proof is the standard inclusion-exclusion sieve on fixed points, expanded with an explicit restriction-extension bijection.

The source records both standard recurrences D_n = nD_{n-1}+(-1)^n and D_n = (n-1)(D_{n-1}+D_{n-2}) with the usual starting ranges, matching the item up to notation and embedding. The local proof derives the first by algebraically splitting the finite alternating formula and the second by eliminating the sign term; that derivation was independently written rather than copied from a located proof.

Increasing and decreasing subsequences of a finite real sequence are standard. The item formalises a sublist as a strictly increasing index map between von Neumann naturals, uses 'sublist' rather than 'subsequence', and explicitly defines pairwise distinctness, so it is a semantic restatement of the standard notions. It has no separate proof component.

The source states that ab+1 distinct reals contain an increasing subsequence of length a+1 or a decreasing one of length b+1. The item extends the conventional positive-parameter statement to all natural m,n, explicitly treating the degenerate cases and expressing subsequences through index maps. The longest-increasing/longest-decreasing rank-pair injection proof is the standard proof, adapted to these conventions.

Sharpness of the mn+1 monotone-subsequence bound via m increasing blocks of n decreasing entries is standard. The item gives an explicit formula for that construction, formalises both sublist bounds, and extends it to zero parameters with an empty-list reading. The proof follows the standard block argument with the local index and pigeonhole APIs made explicit.

Direct arithmetic gives 3^5-3*2^5+3=150. Independently, partitioning all 243 functions by image size gives contributions 0, 3, 90, and the desired three-point-image count, hence 243=93+150.

The standard graph theorem says every finite simple graph with at least two vertices has two vertices of equal degree. The item translates vertices and adjacency into a finite set with a symmetric irreflexive relation, avoiding graph vocabulary; that is a semantic restatement. Its split into the isolated-vertex and universal-degree cases is the standard pigeonhole proof, adapted to relation fibres.

The handshaking identity sum_v deg(v)=2|E| is standard. The item states it without graph primitives, using an irreflexive symmetric relation and unordered two-element subsets, so it is a semantic reformulation. The incidence relation between vertices and unordered related pairs is the standard double-counting proof translated into local notation.

Positive novelty determination: the concrete 17-object, 5-fibre distribution and its accompanying quotient computation are a locally chosen numerical exercise. Direct verification gives 17 <= 5*4 and not 17 <= 5*3, hence ceil(17/5)=4; the strong pigeonhole theorem then supplies a fibre of size at least four. Positive novelty determination: the explicit unequal three-set witness and erroneous term-omission computation are crafted for this page to instantiate the preceding false statement. The three sets have size 3, their pairwise intersections have sizes 2, 1, and 2, their triple intersection has size 1, and their union has size 5; the truncated value is 4, while restoring the triple term gives 5.

Direct counting gives total incidence count 3 and two right fibres, hence average 3/2, while the only fibre cardinalities are 1 and 2; the sourced averaging conclusion 'at least the average' remains true.
